citeAs: Krishna, R., Zhu, Y., Groth, O., Johnson, J., Hata, K., Kravitz, J., Chen, S., Kalantidis, Y., Li, L.-J., Shamma, D. A., Bernstein, M. S., and Fei-Fei, L. (2016). Visual Genome: Connecting Language and Vision Using Crowdsourced Dense Image Annotations. arXiv:1602.07332.
creator: Ranjay Krishna, Yuke Zhu, Oliver Groth, Justin Johnson, Kenji Hata, Joshua Kravitz, Stephanie Chen, Yannis Kalantidis, Li-Jia Li, David A. Shamma, Michael S. Bernstein, Li Fei-Fei (Stanford University, Dresden University of Technology, Yahoo Inc., Snapchat Inc.)
description: Visual Genome is a large-scale dataset of over 108,000 images densely annotated with region descriptions, objects, attributes, relationships, region graphs, scene graphs, and question-answer pairs. Each image contains an average of 21 objects, 18 attributes, 18 pairwise relationships, 42 region descriptions, and 17 QA pairs. All objects, attributes, relationships, and noun phrases are canonicalized to WordNet synsets, enabling structured knowledge representation for cognitive computer vision tasks such as image description and visual question answering.
name: Visual Genome
rai:annotationsPerItem: Each image has on average: 42 region descriptions, 21 objects, 16 attributes, 18 relationships, 17 QA pairs. Verification used 3 unique workers per annotation (majority voting).
rai:annotatorDemographics: Over 33,000 unique crowd workers from Amazon Mechanical Turk. Geographic distribution: United States 93.02%, Philippines 1.29%, Kenya 1.13%, India 0.94%, Russia 0.50%, Canada 0.47%, Others 2.65%. Age range: 18–68 years old, majority between 25–34 years old. Gender: 54.15% male, 45.85% female.
rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: Verification used majority voting (3 workers, 2/3 agreement required) for all components except objects, which used rapid judgments. Canonicalization precision/recall evaluated on held-out samples of 200: Objects: 88.0% precision, 98.5% recall; Attributes: 85.7% precision, 95.9% recall; Relationships: 92.9% precision, 88.5% recall. HITs achieved a 94.1% retention rate. Noun phrase extraction from region descriptions achieved 99% recall on a manually annotated subset of 200 descriptions.
rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: Multiple annotation stages: (1) Region descriptions: workers drew bounding boxes and wrote descriptions; BLEU score thresholds (0.7) enforced diversity; workers shown top 7 most similar prior descriptions to avoid repetition. (2) Objects: workers extracted objects from descriptions and drew tight bounding boxes (coverage + quality requirements). (3) Attributes and relationships: workers added attributes to objects and connected object pairs with relationships based on region descriptions. (4) Scene graphs: region graphs merged by combining co-referenced objects (IoU ≥ 0.8). (5) QA pairs: workers wrote freeform QAs (8 per image, ≥3 different W-types) and region-based QAs. (6) Verification: majority voting (3 workers, 2/3 agreement) for most components; rapid judgments for objects. (7) Canonicalization: all objects, attributes, relationships mapped to WordNet synsets, verified on AMT.
rai:dataBiases: The dataset is somewhat biased towards images of people, as the top synsets include humans playing sports (ski, ballplayer, racket). Images sourced from Flickr via YFCC100M and MS-COCO may reflect the biases of those platforms. Certain sports (skiing, surfboarding) are overrepresented in attribute distributions due to image source bias. The dataset was designed without bias toward a particular task, unlike previous datasets collected for single tasks like image classification.
rai:dataCollection: Visual Genome was collected entirely by crowd workers from Amazon Mechanical Turk (AMT). Over 33,000 unique workers contributed. Approximately 800,000 Human Intelligence Tasks (HITs) were launched on AMT, covering region descriptions, objects, attributes, relationships, region graphs, scene graphs, and question-answer pairs. The dataset was collected over 6 months after 15 months of experimentation and iteration on the data representation. Images were sourced from the intersection of YFCC100M and MS-COCO (108,249 images). Workers earned between $6–$8 per hour.
rai:dataCollectionRawData: 108,249 images from the intersection of YFCC100M (Yahoo Flickr Creative Commons 100M) and MS-COCO datasets. These are real-world, non-iconic images uploaded to Flickr by users, ranging from 72 to 1280 pixels wide with an average width of 500 pixels.
rai:dataCollectionTimeframe: 6 months of data collection after 15 months of experimentation and iteration on the data representation (exact dates not specified).
rai:dataCollectionType: Manual Human Curator, Web Scraping, Crowdsourcing
rai:dataLimitations: The dataset is biased towards images of people and certain sports (skiing, surfboarding) due to the image source (Flickr/YFCC100M/MS-COCO). Canonicalization mappings are imperfect and contain some ambiguity. Relationship classification is difficult due to high intra-class variability. Answers in QA pairs exhibit long-tail distribution. The top 1000 most frequent answers cover only 64.1% of correct answers. Current models trained on the dataset still perform poorly on complex reasoning tasks (e.g., 'why' questions achieve only 3.4% top-100 accuracy).
rai:dataManipulationProtocol: Scene graphs constructed by merging region graph nodes with bounding box overlap-over-union ≥ 0.8 (confirmed by workers). For QA experiments, data split 60% training / 40% test. For attribute/relationship experiments, 80% training / 10% validation / 10% test; random sampling of 500 instances per attribute category for balance. Region descriptions split into 3,150,000 training / 504,420 validation / 504,420 test.
rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: Region descriptions preprocessed by removing non-alphanumeric characters, lowercasing, and stripping excess whitespace. Attributes normalized by morphology (stemming) and mapped to WordNet adjectives. Relationships: prepositions excluded (not in WordNet); verbs mapped to WordNet sentence frames and root hypernyms. Objects, attributes, and relationships canonicalized to WordNet synsets using Stanford NLP tools for noun phrase extraction, with hand-crafted mapping rules for common failure cases (30 for objects, 15 for attributes, 20 for relationships). BLEU score thresholds (0.7) used to enforce diversity in region descriptions.
rai:dataSocialImpact: Visual Genome aims to advance cognitive computer vision tasks beyond simple object recognition toward comprehensive scene understanding, enabling applications such as image search, visual question answering, and robotic interactions. The dataset bridges the gap between perceptual and cognitive AI capabilities.
rai:dataUseCases: Training and benchmarking computer vision models for: image description/captioning, visual question answering, object detection, attribute prediction, relationship prediction/extraction, scene graph generation, semantic image retrieval, dense image captioning, image understanding evaluation, knowledge base construction, action recognition, and robotic interactions.
rai:machineAnnotationTools: Stanford dependency parser (Manning et al., 2014) used to automatically extract nouns from region descriptions as suggestions for workers. Stanford NLP tools used for noun phrase extraction during canonicalization. BLEU score (Papineni et al., 2002) used programmatically to enforce description diversity. word2vec (Mikolov et al., 2013) used for semantic analysis of descriptions. WordNet (Miller, 1995) used for canonicalization of all objects, attributes, and relationships.

null_reasons.rai:dataCollectionMissingData: Paper does not explicitly discuss missing data handling in the collection process.
null_reasons.rai:dataImputationProtocol: No imputation protocol described; missing values are handled by exclusion (e.g., descriptions with no objects have no region graphs), not imputation.
null_reasons.rai:personalSensitiveInformation: Paper does not discuss collection of personal or sensitive information about image subjects.
null_reasons.rai:dataReleaseMaintenancePlan: Paper does not describe a versioning or maintenance plan beyond mentioning the first release.
